subject: Banking
title: Bretton Woods and the Dollar
description: A short lesson to help you apply Bretton Woods and the Dollar.

hook.text: In 1944, 44 nations met in New Hampshire and agreed to make the US dollar the center of global finance.

buildup.text: Every currency was pegged to the dollar. The dollar was pegged to gold at $35 per ounce.

discovery.text: Bretton Woods created the IMF, the World Bank, and a stable global monetary system. It rebuilt the postwar economy.

twist.text: In 1971, Nixon ended gold convertibility. The dollar became fiat money. Bretton Woods collapsed after just 27 years.

climax.text: The system that stabilized the world economy was abandoned because America couldn't back every dollar with gold.

punchline.text: 44 nations agreed. 27 years later, Nixon pulled the plug on gold.

quiz.question: What ended the Bretton Woods system?

details.summary: The 1944 Bretton Woods agreement established the US dollar as the world's reserve currency backed by gold, creating a fixed exchange rate system that underpinned global trade until President Nixon ended gold convertibility in 1971.
details.whyItMatters: Bretton Woods made the dollar the center of global finance, a privileged position America retains today. The system's rules and its eventual collapse shaped every aspect of modern international banking and trade.
takeaways: 44 nations agreed to peg their currencies to the dollar at fixed rates
The dollar was convertible to gold at $35 per ounce
Nixon ended gold convertibility in 1971, creating today's floating rate system

faq.question: Why did the Bretton Woods system collapse?
faq.answer: America printed too many dollars to fund the Vietnam War and domestic spending. Foreign governments began exchanging dollars for gold, draining US reserves. Nixon ended convertibility rather than cut spending, ending the system.

faq.question: Why is the dollar still the world's reserve currency after Bretton Woods ended?
faq.answer: The dollar's deep and liquid markets, US military power, rule of law, and the inertia of global trade pricing in dollars sustain its dominance. No alternative currency has the combination of stability and liquidity to replace it.
